newsitem.title: USA: Dow open seen mixed to steady.
newsitem.headline: Dow open seen mixed to steady.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to start mixed to higher on Wednesday a day after taking a breather from its record-breaking run.

Analysts said the Dow Jones industrial average likely would rebound on a day slowed by investors taking an early start to the Thankgiving holiday. The Dow closed at 6528, down 19 from Monday's record close.
Another guide for the market will be a revision to the third-quarter gross domestic product and weekly jobless claims, both due out shortly.
"I think we'll have a mixed opening and we'll finish up for the day," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.
He added, "It doesn't dip down too long before coming back."
Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said higher bond prices overnight suggested a rebound in the Dow if no shocks emerged from U.S. economic data.
The government's revised third-quarter report, issued at 8:30 a.m. EST, put GDP growth for the period at two percent, against a previous figure of 2.2 percent.
Jobless claims for the week ending Nov 23 were 336,250, unchanged from the prior week.
"Bond prices are up half a point, which suggests we are headed for a higher opening provided there are no bumps from the day's economic data," Cardillo said.
In London, the FTSE 100 dropped 11 points to 4057. U.S. stocks were steady to slightly higher in London, with dealing expected to remain quiet in view of the Thanksgiving break.

In Tokyo, stocks ended on a feeble tone, mostly to profit-taking after the Nikkei average had risen for three straight sessions. The impact of the Bank of Japan's "Tankan" business sentiment survey was limited, and the Nikkei-225 ended down 72.97 points or 0.34 percent at 21,345.28.
After the U.S. data were released, the long bond modestly extended its gains, up 20/32 to yield 6.40 percent.
"It's a continuation of the kind of numbers we have been getting. The way this long bond looks, it can get to a six percent yield by the end of the year," Brown said.

"The market is not paying a whole lot of attention to interest rates recently, though the decline in the yield has been a nice prop. The big single plus has been the astounding amount of money still flowing into the market, the minus is money managers are running free cash reserves to the lowest levels I've seen." He saw a firmer open and a quieter day.
U.S. Treasuries were higher. The benchmark 30-year bond rose 22/32, to yield 6.39 percent.
The dollar firmed in Japan to 113.
The December S&P 500 future rose 1.0 points to 758.35.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column reported China's stock market has roared to life on a vague hope regulators will no longer enforce restrictions preventing local investors from buying shares designated for foreigners.

In the United States, Chiron Corp's stock fell 17 percent following a failed clinical trial for a new vaccine, but analysts said the news was not completely negative. They say the stock, which closed at 18-7/8, is now cheap enough to consider buying, The New York Times reported in its Market Place column.
-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730
